Call a position at the start of Bob’s turn safe if Bob has a strategy that guarantees termination against every subsequent sequence of Alice’s moves.

We use the following switching lemma for this game.

Lemma. If a finite position at the start of Bob’s turn is safe, then every legal move of Bob leads to a safe position at the start of Alice’s next turn.

Proof of the lemma. Suppose that Bob’s legal move replaces an even entry x by x/2 and that the resulting position were unsafe. Then Alice has a continuation producing an infinite play from that position. Prepend the move x→x/2 to that continuation. At the preceding Bob-turn position, Bob could therefore choose this move and then follow the alleged infinite continuation. Since Alice’s prior move is arbitrary, this contradicts safety. Thus the resulting position is safe. ∎

The initial position is safe by hypothesis: Bob can force termination regardless of Alice’s moves. Consider any play in which Bob makes arbitrary legal moves. After each Alice move, the current position is safe, because safety is preserved through Alice’s move by the hypothesis that Bob’s strategy works against every Alice move; after each legal Bob move, safety is preserved by the lemma. Hence every position reached at the start of Bob’s turn is safe.

If the displayed play were infinite, it would give an infinite continuation from the initial position, contradicting the meaning of safety. Therefore every play is finite, and it ends precisely when Bob has no legal move, that is, when all board entries are odd. Hence the game is guaranteed to end regardless of either player’s choices. ∎

Let a Bob-turn position be called winning if Bob has some strategy that makes the game end after finitely many further moves, whatever Alice does.

The hypothesis says that the initial position is winning. We need show that no arbitrary play from it can be infinite.

We use the following elementary closure fact: whenever a Bob-turn position is winning, every legal Bob move from it leaves a winning position. Indeed, if a legal move led to a position from which Alice could produce an infinite play, Bob could choose that legal move and then Alice’s infinite continuation would defeat his supposed winning strategy. This contradicts that the original position is winning.

Now follow any play. After Alice’s move, the resulting Bob-turn position is still winning, because the definition of winning quantifies over every Alice move. Bob then makes an arbitrary legal move, and the closure fact shows that the next position is again winning. Inductively, every position encountered while the play continues is winning.

An infinite play would itself be an infinite continuation from the initial winning position, which is impossible. Thus every play terminates. Since the only terminal condition is that Bob has no even integer to halve, the game ends for every possible sequence of Alice’s and Bob’s moves. ∎

Define W to be the set of positions at the beginning of Bob’s turn from which Bob can force termination against every Alice strategy. The initial position belongs to W by assumption.

We first verify the required closure property. Let P∈W, and let Bob make any legal move from P, producing Q. If Q∉W, then by definition Bob cannot force termination from Q; equivalently, Alice has a continuation from Q along which the game never ends. Bob could choose the move P→Q and then face that continuation. This would show that P∉W, a contradiction. Therefore every legal Bob successor of a position in W is again in W.

Also, every possible Alice move from a position in W leads to a Bob-turn position in W: this is exactly what it means for Bob’s forcing strategy to work regardless of Alice’s move.

Take an arbitrary play from the initial position. Starting in W, after every Alice move the position remains in W, and after every arbitrary legal Bob move it remains in W by the closure property. If the play never ended, it would be an infinite continuation from the initial position, contradicting that the initial position lies in W. Consequently all plays are finite. The game ends when Bob has no valid move, so the asserted guarantee holds for all choices by both players. ∎

The initial position P₀ lies in W by hypothesis.

We require two dependency facts. First, if P∈W, then every position obtained from P by one possible Alice move lies in W, since Bob’s guarantee is uniform over Alice’s choices. Second, if P∈W and Q is obtained from P by any legal Bob move, then Q∈W. For if Q∉W, there would be a continuation from Q in which the game does not terminate. Bob could choose P→Q and then that continuation would give a nonterminating continuation from P, contradicting P∈W.

Now let both players choose moves arbitrarily. Inductively, after each Alice move and each legal Bob move, the current Bob-turn position remains in W. Thus every finite prefix of the arbitrary play can be extended only from a position with a termination guarantee. If the play were infinite, its tail would be a nonterminating continuation from P₀, contradicting P₀∈W.

Therefore no infinite play exists. Every play is finite and must stop when Bob has no legal move, namely when every integer on the board is odd. Hence the game is guaranteed to end regardless of Alice’s or Bob’s moves. ∎
